found-assessment-l01.q: You are dispatched for a single patient struck by a car. On arrival you count three injured people on the roadway. Which resource request is the first priority?
choices: A supervisor to write the report
At least two more ambulances, then begin triage
The utility company for the damaged light pole
A tow truck for the vehicle
found-assessment-l01.why: Three or more patients exceeds one crew, so transport resources and triage come first. The pole and the vehicle are scene problems that do not move patients.

found-assessment-l01.q: A partner says 'scene is safe' at the front door and never mentions it again during a 20-minute call. What is wrong with that?
choices: Nothing, safety is determined once on arrival
Safety only has to be stated to dispatch
Scene safety is reassessed continuously, because a safe scene can turn unsafe at any moment
Safety statements are only required on trauma calls
found-assessment-l01.why: A quiet apartment changes when someone comes home or a patient becomes violent. Safety is a running judgment, not a one-time box, and you should know your exit before you kneel down.

found-assessment-l02.q: An adult is breathing 4 times per minute with barely visible chest rise. How many breaths per minute do you deliver with a bag-valve mask?
found-assessment-l02.why: One breath every 6 seconds equals 10 per minute. Faster bagging inflates the stomach and drops venous return; slower does not clear the carbon dioxide.

found-assessment-l02.q: You expose a trauma patient, complete your sweep, and leave him uncovered on a 12 C night so you can keep watching the chest. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, visualization is more important than temperature
Cold impairs clotting and worsens bleeding, so covering the patient is part of the treatment
It only matters if the patient reports feeling cold
It only matters in patients over 65
found-assessment-l02.why: Hypothermia is one leg of the trauma death spiral with bleeding and acidosis. The E in XABCDE is expose and environment, and the blanket is the environment half.

found-assessment-l03.q: A 70 kg adult has lost about 25 percent of his blood volume. What does a systolic of 118 mmHg tell you?
choices: Blood loss has been overestimated
Perfusion is adequate and no urgent action is needed
Very little, because a healthy adult can lose about 30 percent before the systolic falls
The patient is hypertensive at baseline
found-assessment-l03.why: Blood pressure is the last compensatory mechanism to fail. Heart rate, skin, and mental status already changed, and waiting for a pressure drop means waiting for decompensation.

found-assessment-l03.q: Which of these is the clearest stay-and-play situation?
choices: A hypoglycemic patient who is awake, can swallow, and responds to oral glucose
A gunshot wound to the abdomen with a weak radial pulse
A stroke patient 40 minutes from last known well
Chest pain with ST elevation on a medic monitor
found-assessment-l03.why: Hypoglycemia is a problem you can actually fix where the patient is. Penetrating torso trauma, stroke in the window, and a heart attack all need an operating room, a scanner, or a cath lab, so they are load-and-go.

found-assessment-l04.q: You ask about allergies and the patient says no. Later the hospital finds a penicillin allergy from childhood. What should you have asked?
choices: Whether she has seasonal allergies
Whether any family member has drug allergies
Whether she has ever had a bad reaction to a medication, and what the reaction was
Nothing more, patients are responsible for their own history
found-assessment-l04.why: Patients forget reactions they think of as old or minor. Asking about reactions rather than the word allergy recovers the information, and asking what happened separates true allergy from side effect.

found-assessment-l04.q: A patient says her chest pain is a 7 out of 10 now and was a 9 out of 10 an hour ago. Which two OPQRST letters did she just answer?
choices: O and P
S and T
Q and R
P and Q
found-assessment-l04.why: Severity is the 0 to 10 rating and time covers duration and direction of change. Onset is how it began, quality is the character, and region is location and radiation.

found-assessment-l05.q: A patient has abdominal pain in the right lower quadrant. In what order do you palpate the four quadrants?
choices: Right lower first, then the rest
All four at once with both hands
The three other quadrants first, then the right lower last
Only the painful quadrant
found-assessment-l05.why: Pressing the painful quadrant first triggers guarding that makes the rest of the exam unreadable. You save the painful area for last so the earlier findings are honest.

found-assessment-l05.q: You splint a deformed forearm. The patient's fingers are now cool and the radial pulse is gone. What is your first action?
choices: Loosen or reapply the splint and recheck pulse, motor, and sensation
Elevate the arm and continue transport
Apply a cold pack to the fingers
Document the finding and reassess in 15 minutes
found-assessment-l05.why: A pulse that was present before splinting and absent after means the splint is compressing the vessel. You fix the splint immediately; ice, elevation, and waiting do nothing for a compromised circulation.

found-assessment-l06.q: A patient's blood glucose reads 54 mg/dL. He is awake and can swallow. What does this number mean and what does it earn him?
choices: Normal, no action needed
Hypoglycemia, and oral glucose of about 15 g since he can protect his airway
Hyperglycemia, and immediate transport only
An unreliable reading that should be ignored
found-assessment-l06.why: Below 70 mg/dL is hypoglycemia, and it is a reversible cause of altered mental status. An awake patient who can swallow gets oral glucose; an unresponsive one does not, because of aspiration risk.

found-assessment-l06.q: You tell a patient 'I am going to count your breathing now' and then count 24 per minute. What is the problem with that number?
choices: It is too fast to count accurately
Respiratory rate should always be counted for a full minute
People change their breathing when they know they are being watched, so the number is not a true resting rate
The number is fine, announcing it makes no difference
found-assessment-l06.why: Breathing is partly voluntary, so awareness distorts it. Count for 30 seconds and double it while appearing to still hold the pulse.

found-assessment-l07.q: A 62-year-old crashed his car into a pole with no skid marks and says he does not remember the last few minutes. Which flow do you run?
choices: Trauma only, because there was a crash
Medical only, because he blacked out
Neither, transport without assessment
Both: trauma exam for the crash plus glucose, stroke screen, and cardiac history for the cause
found-assessment-l07.why: A crash with no evasive action suggests a medical event caused it. Committing to one path guarantees you miss either the injuries or the syncope, seizure, stroke, or low sugar behind them.

found-assessment-l07.q: Which statement about history timing is correct?
choices: Trauma patients get a full history before any exam
Responsive medical patients get the history before the focused exam; significant trauma patients get the exam first and a shorter history later
Medical patients never need a physical exam
History always comes after vital signs in both flows
found-assessment-l07.why: In medical calls the story points at the system to examine. In significant trauma the mechanism decides the exam, and the history, especially blood thinners, is collected while moving.

found-assessment-l08.q: An alert, sober 30-year-old with a minor forearm laceration wants to refuse transport. He repeats back that the cut could get infected and could involve a tendon. What is missing before you leave?
choices: Nothing, he clearly has capacity
A family member's signature
A signed refusal with a witness signature, plus documented alternatives such as calling back or seeing his own doctor today
Medical control approval for every refusal
found-assessment-l08.why: He has capacity and understood the risks, so the remaining steps are alternatives and a signed, witnessed refusal. Family cannot sign for a competent adult, and medical control is contacted for high-risk refusals rather than every one.

found-assessment-l08.q: An 80-year-old who has lived alone independently is brought in confused after two days of burning on urination. Which part of AEIOU-TIPS fits best?
choices: P, psychiatric
I, infection
E, epilepsy
A, alcohol
found-assessment-l08.why: New confusion in an older adult is most often infection, and urinary tract infection is the classic source. Calling it psychiatric or intoxication in a previously independent elder is exactly the assumption that gets people hurt.

found-assessment-l09.q: A 58-year-old has a headache that started suddenly and is the worst of his life. Which focused exam items matter most?
choices: Mental status, pupils, facial droop with arm drift and speech, neck stiffness, and blood pressure
Abdominal quadrants and last oral intake
Pulse-motor-sensation in all four limbs only
Lung sounds at four points and neck veins
found-assessment-l09.why: The worst thing a sudden severe headache can be is a bleed in the brain, a stroke, or meningitis, so the exam targets neurologic function, meningeal signs, and pressure. Chest and abdominal exams do not address any of those.

found-assessment-l09.q: Two patients say 'chest pain.' One is 22 and it hurts when you press the sternum after lifting weights. One is 72, diabetic, gray and sweaty. Why do the exams differ?
choices: Because older patients always get more testing
Because you pick the exam from the worst thing the complaint could be in that particular patient
Because chest wall pain is not a real complaint
Because only patients over 65 can have heart attacks
found-assessment-l09.why: The complaint is a doorway, not a destination. Reproducible pain in a young lifter points at the chest wall; the same words in a gray diabetic point at a heart attack and earn lung sounds, both arm pulses, neck veins, legs, and a fast trip.

found-assessment-l10.q: A 3-year-old weighs in with a blood pressure of 72/44 after a fall. Using the age-based floor, how do you read that systolic?
choices: Normal, the floor is 70 mmHg at any pediatric age
Hypotensive, because the floor is about 76 mmHg for a 3-year-old
Too high for age
Unreadable without a weight
found-assessment-l10.why: The floor is 70 plus twice the age in years, which gives about 76 mmHg here, so 72 is hypotension and a very late finding in a child. A single fixed floor of 70 applies only around age 1.

found-assessment-l10.q: A daughter says her 79-year-old father 'has been a little off since yesterday.' He is oriented to person and place but not time. What is your first move?
choices: Chart dementia and transport routinely
Reassure the family this is normal aging
Establish his baseline from the family, then check glucose, temperature, oxygen, and medications
Ask him to repeat three words and nothing further
found-assessment-l10.why: Confused means nothing until you know what he was like yesterday. A change over one day is delirium, which is an acute emergency most often from infection, hypoxia, low sugar, a medication, or a bleed.

found-assessment-l11.q: A man is unresponsive in a closed garage with a car engine running. What changes about your approach?
choices: Nothing, treat him where he lies
Only the oxygen device you choose
Ask the family to open a window before you enter
The scene is unsafe: the space is ventilated and the patient is moved to fresh air before assessment continues
found-assessment-l11.why: Carbon monoxide is invisible and will drop a rescuer as fast as a patient. Scene safety reverts to the top of the list, and his pulse oximeter reading will also be falsely high.

found-assessment-l11.q: Which pair of findings points toward a metabolic cause rather than a structural one?
choices: Symmetric reactive pupils with equal movement on both sides
One dilated unreactive pupil with one-sided arm weakness
A facial droop with slurred speech
A depressed area of skull with clear fluid from an ear
found-assessment-l11.why: Symmetry suggests the whole brain is affected equally, which is what sugar, drugs, and infection do. Asymmetry, skull findings, and one-sided deficits suggest a bleed or other structural lesion.

found-assessment-l12.q: A bleeding wound sits in the groin crease, too high for a limb tourniquet. What do you do?
choices: Apply a tourniquet across the pelvis
Pack the wound with gauze and hold hard direct pressure
Elevate the leg and apply a cold pack
Apply a pressure dressing and reassess in 10 minutes
found-assessment-l12.why: Junctional sites at the groin, armpit, and neck cannot take a limb tourniquet, so wound packing with sustained hard pressure is the answer. Elevation and cold do not control arterial bleeding.

found-assessment-l12.q: Two EMTs stand over a critical trauma patient and both reach for the legs. What went wrong?
choices: Nothing, duplicated effort is safe
They should both start at the head
Roles were never assigned out loud, so nobody owns the head, the airway, or bleeding control
They should wait for a third provider before touching the patient
found-assessment-l12.why: Spoken role assignment, one provider on head and airway and one on body, bleeding, exposure, and vitals, is what prevents an unheld head and an uncontrolled bleed. Ambiguity is what costs the minutes.

found-assessment-l13.q: A blood pressure moves from 130/70 to 122/96 over 12 minutes. Calculate the pulse pressures and say what happened.
choices: 60 then 26; the patient is vasoconstricting, which is compensated shock
60 then 26; the patient is improving
70 then 30; the patient is dehydrated only
The pulse pressure cannot be calculated from these numbers
found-assessment-l13.why: Systolic minus diastolic gives 60 then 26. A narrowing pulse pressure means the vessels are clamping down to hold pressure, and that is compensated shock before the systolic ever falls.

found-assessment-l13.q: Which pairing of numbers is the most ominous combination in a bleeding patient?
choices: Rising heart rate with a stable blood pressure
Falling heart rate with a falling blood pressure and declining mental status
Rising respiratory rate with warm skin
Stable heart rate with a rising temperature
found-assessment-l13.why: A heart rate that finally slows while the pressure keeps dropping is the pump giving up, not recovery. Rising heart rate with a held pressure is compensation still working, which is worrying but not peri-arrest.

found-assessment-l14.q: A stroke patient knows exactly what he wants to say but can only produce two or three words and is visibly frustrated. How do you get information?
choices: Speak louder and repeat the question faster
Ask yes-or-no questions confirmed by a hand squeeze, and give him time without interrupting
Ask only open questions so he can explain fully
Skip the history and rely on the physical exam alone
found-assessment-l14.why: Expressive aphasia leaves comprehension intact, so yes-or-no questions with a second channel work. Volume does not help comprehension, open questions demand the exact ability he lost, and interrupting resets the whole attempt.

found-assessment-l14.q: A patient is transferred from a nursing facility. Which paperwork is most useful to take with you?
choices: The activities calendar and the meal plan
The visitor log
The face sheet and the medication administration record, plus any DNR or POLST form
The facility's inspection certificate
found-assessment-l14.why: The face sheet carries baseline, diagnoses, and contacts, the medication record shows what was actually given and when, and the DNR or POLST changes what you are allowed to do. Nothing else on that list is clinical.

found-assessment-l15.q: You start your report while your crew slides the patient onto the hospital bed. What should change?
choices: Give the report once, to the person taking over, after the move, so it is actually heard
Speak louder so it carries over the transfer
Give the report twice, once during and once after
Write it down instead and hand it over without speaking
found-assessment-l15.why: Nobody absorbs a verbal report during a physical move. One report, to the person who owns the patient, in a moment quiet enough to hear it, is what survives the handoff.

found-assessment-l15.q: Which chart line will read worst if it is quoted back in a deposition?
choices: Patient declined the cardiac monitor after risks were explained
BP unobtainable due to bilateral arm injuries; radial pulse strong and regular
Patient was noncompliant and rude throughout the call
Speaks in three-word sentences, SpO2 89 percent on room air at 1412
found-assessment-l15.why: That line is an opinion about the patient, not an observation, and it does nothing clinically. The other three are facts, explained gaps, or documented decisions, all of which are defensible.

found-assessment-l16.q: You palpate the pelvis during the station, find it stable, and say nothing. What happens to that point?
choices: It is awarded because the action was observed
It is lost, because the evaluator scores the stated finding, not the motion
It is awarded if you mention it in the final summary
It does not exist on the skill sheet
found-assessment-l16.why: The sheet scores actions and findings that the evaluator can see and hear. Say both together: palpating the pelvis once for instability, it is stable.

found-assessment-l16.q: Halfway through the station you realize you never stated the spinal precautions decision. What is the best move?
choices: Continue and hope the evaluator did not notice
Stop the station and restart from the beginning
Mention it only in your closing summary
Say aloud that you are addressing it now, then state your decision and the reason
found-assessment-l16.why: Recovering aloud costs nothing and evaluators score sheet items, not elegance. Restarting is not an option and hoping leaves an unscored item blank.

quiz.q: You arrive at a house fire where a firefighter has carried a patient to the sidewalk. Smoke is still pouring from the front door. Where do you assess the patient?
choices: At the sidewalk or further away, in the cold zone
Just inside the front door to stay out of the weather
In the doorway so fire can hand off more patients quickly
On the front porch next to the hose line
quiz.why: Scene safety governs where care happens, and smoke, heat, and collapse risk make anywhere near the structure the wrong place. Convenience, weather, and handoff speed never justify assessing a patient inside a hazard zone.

quiz.q: During a size-up at a rollover crash you state BSI, scene safety, mechanism, and patient count. Which two scored items are still missing?
choices: Chief complaint and SAMPLE history
Additional resources needed and the spinal precautions decision
Baseline vitals and glucose
Transport destination and hospital notification
quiz.why: Size-up has six scored parts, and resources plus the spinal decision are the two you skipped. History, vitals, and destination all belong to later phases of the assessment.

quiz.q: You are assisting with suctioning a vomiting patient in the back of the ambulance wearing only gloves. What is the deficiency?
choices: You should be wearing a gown for all patient contact
Gloves are not required during suctioning
Eye protection and a mask are indicated because splashing is likely
An N95 respirator is required for all vomiting patients
quiz.why: Standard precautions scale with the exposure: fluid that can splash earns eye protection and a mask. Gowns are for childbirth and heavy bleeding, and N95 respirators are for suspected airborne disease such as tuberculosis, not vomiting.

quiz.q: A 19-year-old is unresponsive after a dive into shallow water. You need to open his airway. Which maneuver and why?
choices: Head-tilt chin-lift, because it is the most effective
No airway maneuver until a collar is applied
Head-tilt chin-lift with the head turned to the side
Jaw thrust, because the mechanism could have injured the cervical spine
quiz.why: A diving mechanism loads the neck, so the jaw thrust opens the airway without extending it. Delaying the airway for a collar and turning the head are both worse, and a head-tilt in this patient risks moving an unstable spine.

quiz.q: You apply a tourniquet high on a thigh at 1418 and bleeding stops. What must happen next regarding the tourniquet?
choices: Write 1418 on the tourniquet and in the chart, and leave it in place
Loosen it every 10 minutes to restore some circulation
Cover it with a blanket so the patient does not see it
Remove it once the patient's pressure normalizes
quiz.why: The application time drives every hospital decision about the limb, and it must be visible and charted. Periodic loosening restarts the bleeding, covering it hides it from the receiving team, and field release in a bleeding patient is not an EMT decision.

quiz.q: During the primary survey of an adult you find capillary refill of 4 seconds, cool skin, and a weak radial pulse. What does this section of XABCDE tell you?
choices: Airway compromise is developing
Circulation is impaired and perfusion is failing
Disability from a head injury is present
Exposure has made the patient hypothermic and nothing more
quiz.why: Delayed refill with cool skin and a weak pulse is the C of XABCDE: the body is shunting blood away from the periphery. Cold surroundings can prolong refill, but not alongside a weak pulse in a patient who was warm a minute ago.

quiz.q: From the doorway you see a woman sitting bolt upright, leaning on her hands, gray, speaking three words at a time. What have you just completed?
choices: A secondary assessment
A SAMPLE history
A general impression, the first step of the primary survey
A reassessment
quiz.why: The general impression is formed before you touch the patient and already tells you she is sick. The secondary exam, history, and reassessment all come later and all require patient contact.

quiz.q: A 48-year-old with crushing chest pain is diaphoretic and says 'something is very wrong, I think I am dying.' How should you weigh that statement?
choices: Discount it as anxiety about the ambulance
Treat it as a reason to give reassurance and slow down
Record it in the chart but do not let it change priority
Treat a sense of impending doom as a real clinical finding that raises priority
quiz.why: Patients who say they are dying are frequently right, and the statement pairs with real physiology in heart attack, aortic dissection, and anaphylaxis. Dismissing it as anxiety or charting it without acting is how a high-priority patient gets treated as routine.

quiz.q: A critical trauma patient needs ALS. The medic unit is 15 minutes away, you are 10 minutes from the trauma center, and the patient is packaged. What do you do?
choices: Begin transport now and request an intercept en route in case the medics can meet you
Remain on scene until the medic unit arrives
Cancel the trauma center and go to the closest urgent care
Wait 5 minutes and reassess before deciding
quiz.why: The hospital is closer than the paramedics, so driving is the fastest route to everything the patient needs. Waiting on scene burns minutes against the 10-minute benchmark, and a critical trauma patient is not an urgent care patient.

quiz.q: Which patient is best described as 'not sick' on your first impression?
choices: A 60-year-old who is mottled at the knees with a heart rate of 46
A 25-year-old with an obviously deformed wrist, warm dry skin, alert and oriented, complaining bitterly about the pain
A 40-year-old sitting in tripod position speaking two words at a time
A 72-year-old who is newly confused with cool clammy skin
quiz.why: Painful is not the same as sick. Warm dry skin, full sentences, and a normal mental status mean perfusion is intact. Mottling with bradycardia, tripoding, and new confusion with clammy skin are all perfusion or oxygenation failures.

quiz.q: A patient with shortness of breath tells you she cannot walk to the bathroom without stopping, though last week she could climb a flight of stairs. Which part of the history is this?
choices: Allergies
Last oral intake
Severity and time under OPQRST, applied to breathlessness
Past medical history
quiz.why: OPQRST works for shortness of breath as well as pain, and exercise tolerance now versus a week ago is severity plus trend. Allergies, intake, and past history are SAMPLE items that do not describe the complaint itself.

quiz.q: Which of these belongs under the M of SAMPLE and is most likely to be forgotten by the patient?
choices: The blood pressure pill she takes every morning
The insulin she injects twice a day
The antibiotic she finished last week
The over-the-counter ibuprofen and the herbal supplement she takes daily
quiz.why: Patients routinely think medications means prescriptions only, so non-prescription drugs and supplements go unreported even though ibuprofen affects bleeding and kidneys. The prescribed items on the list are the ones patients do remember.

quiz.q: Which of these is a sign rather than a symptom?
choices: A respiratory rate of 28 with visible retractions
Nausea
Dizziness
A burning sensation in the chest
quiz.why: A sign is something you can observe or measure yourself. Nausea, dizziness, and a burning sensation exist only in the patient's report, which makes them symptoms.

quiz.q: During a rapid trauma assessment you feel a crackling under the skin of the upper chest, like bubble wrap. What does this most likely indicate?
choices: Normal muscle tone
Air leaking into the tissues, which suggests an airway or lung injury
A superficial bruise
Dehydration of the skin
quiz.why: Subcutaneous air means air has escaped from the airway or lung into the soft tissue, which flags a serious chest injury. Bruises, muscle, and dry skin do not crackle under your fingers.

quiz.q: A 35-year-old fell 8 feet from a ladder, is alert and oriented times four, sober, and complains only of right ankle pain with a normal neuro exam. Which exam is indicated?
choices: Full rapid head-to-toe because any fall is significant
No exam at all, splint and go
Focused exam of the ankle plus the joint above and below, with pulse, motor, and sensation
Head-to-toe plus a pelvis check and a log roll
quiz.why: Eight feet is below the adult 20-foot threshold and the patient is a reliable reporter with a normal exam, so a focused exam fits. Skipping the exam entirely misses vessel or nerve injury, and a full sweep here spends time without a mechanism to justify it.

quiz.q: Which of these is a significant mechanism of injury for a 4-year-old who is 40 inches tall?
choices: A fall from a 3-foot couch onto carpet
Tripping while running on a flat sidewalk
Falling off a 2-foot step stool
A fall of 11 feet from a second-story window
quiz.why: For children the threshold is greater than 10 feet or more than three times the child's height, which is about 10 feet here, so 11 feet qualifies. The other falls are short and low-energy and do not by themselves buy a full-body sweep.

quiz.q: A patient with a stab wound to the left upper back was never log-rolled because he was found supine and denies back pain. What is the most likely consequence?
choices: A posterior wound, and the bleeding from it, goes unfound
No consequence, since he would report a wound he could feel
Only a delay in documentation
An increased risk of hypothermia and nothing else
quiz.why: The back is the single most skipped region and is where posterior penetrating wounds hide. Adrenaline, distracting injuries, and intoxication all make pain reporting unreliable, so the one controlled log roll is how you actually see that surface.

quiz.q: You obtain vitals at 1400 on a stable patient with an ankle injury, then transport for 35 minutes. How many further sets should appear in the chart at minimum?
choices: None, one set is enough for a stable patient
Two, at roughly 1415 and 1430
Six, one every 5 minutes
One, taken on arrival at the hospital
quiz.why: Stable patients get reassessed every 15 minutes, which produces two more sets over 35 minutes, plus one immediately after splinting. A single set gives nobody a trend, and 5-minute intervals belong to unstable patients.

quiz.q: An unresponsive 55-year-old has a pulse oximeter reading of 97 percent on room air and is breathing 8 times per minute with shallow chest rise. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Oxygenation and ventilation are both adequate
Oxygen should be withheld since the saturation is high
The saturation is adequate right now but ventilation is failing, so assisted breaths are needed
The oximeter is broken and should be replaced before acting
quiz.why: Pulse oximetry measures oxygen carried, not carbon dioxide cleared, so a good number can coexist with dangerous hypoventilation. A rate of 8 with poor tidal volume earns bag-valve-mask ventilation at 1 breath every 6 seconds.

quiz.q: You check pupils on an unresponsive patient: both are 2 mm and sluggish, equal to each other. Which finding is this closest to?
choices: PERRL, entirely normal
A blown pupil from rising intracranial pressure
Stimulant intoxication
Pinpoint pupils, which raise suspicion for opioids
quiz.why: Small, symmetric, sluggish pupils fit an opioid effect, especially paired with slow breathing. PERRL requires brisk reactivity, a blown pupil is unilateral and dilated, and stimulants dilate rather than constrict.

quiz.q: You assist ventilations on a patient breathing 6 per minute. When is the next reassessment due?
choices: Immediately, because reassessment follows every intervention
In 5 minutes, on the unstable schedule only
In 15 minutes, since a treatment was already given
On arrival at the hospital
quiz.why: Every intervention is followed by an immediate check of whether it worked, on top of the scheduled interval. Waiting 5 or 15 minutes to learn that your mask seal is failing wastes exactly the time the patient does not have.

quiz.q: An alert 45-year-old cut his hand on a table saw. Bleeding is controlled with a pressure dressing. What comes next?
choices: A rapid head-to-toe assessment with DCAP-BTLS
A focused exam of the hand and forearm with pulse, motor, and sensation, plus a SAMPLE history
A log roll to inspect the back
A full spinal immobilization
quiz.why: This is an isolated injury in a reliable patient, so the exam goes where the injury is and the history covers tetanus status, blood thinners, and hand dominance. Full sweeps, log rolls, and spinal packaging need a mechanism that loaded the spine.

quiz.q: Which patient's assessment should proceed exam first, history second?
choices: An alert 50-year-old with two hours of abdominal pain
An alert 30-year-old with a migraine
An unresponsive 60-year-old found alone in a locked apartment
An alert 70-year-old with a two-day cough and fever
quiz.why: With no history obtainable, your hands and meters do the work first and the story is assembled afterward from bystanders, bottles, and bracelets. The three alert medical patients can all tell you their story, so history comes first and directs the exam.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old diabetic drove into a parked car at low speed. He is alert but sweaty and says he 'felt funny' just before. What is the single most valuable early test?
choices: Palpating the pelvis
Counting respirations for a full minute
Measuring the vehicle intrusion
A blood glucose reading
quiz.why: Feeling funny before a crash in a diabetic points at hypoglycemia as the cause of the crash, and it is reversible in minutes. The other options are either part of a trauma exam he also needs or scene documentation, but none of them changes the next five minutes.

quiz.q: A 35-year-old with a known seizure disorder is postictal, sleepy, and confused 4 minutes after a witnessed seizure. Which letter of AEIOU-TIPS fits and what do you still check?
choices: E for epilepsy, and you still check glucose and sweep for injuries from the seizure
O for overdose, and you give naloxone
U for uremia, and you ask about dialysis only
P for psychiatric, and no further workup is needed
quiz.why: A known seizure disorder fits E, but postictal confusion has the same look as hypoglycemia, and seizing patients strike their heads and dislocate shoulders. Assuming overdose, kidney failure, or a psychiatric cause here skips the two checks that actually matter.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old with a swollen wrist wants to refuse transport. Her parents cannot be reached and she is alert and oriented. What applies?
choices: She may refuse because she understands the risks
She is a minor and generally cannot refuse; contact medical direction and follow protocol for unreachable guardians
A neighbor may sign the refusal on her behalf
Refusal is valid once you document that she is oriented times four
quiz.why: Capacity requires an adult or an emancipated minor, so orientation alone does not make her refusal valid. A neighbor has no legal authority, and medical direction exists precisely for this situation.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient has a medical alert bracelet, a dialysis fistula in the left forearm, and a fruity odor on the breath. Which finding narrows your differential fastest?
choices: The bracelet alone
The fistula alone
All three together, because they name likely metabolic causes to check with a glucose and a careful history
None of them, since only vital signs matter
quiz.why: The bracelet, the fistula, and the breath odor each point at a metabolic cause, and together they steer you toward glucose, ketoacidosis, and missed dialysis. Treating physical clues as decoration in a patient who cannot speak throws away the only history available.

quiz.q: You are documenting a high-risk refusal by a competent adult who fell from a roof. Which entry best protects the patient and you?
choices: Patient refused. Signature obtained.
Patient refused against advice. Crew departed.
Patient refused. Family present.
Patient stated 'I could have a bleed in my head or my belly and I could die.' Alternatives offered, medical direction contacted at 1512, refusal signed and witnessed by Officer Ruiz.
quiz.why: Informed refusal is shown by the patient repeating the specific risks back, plus alternatives, medical direction, and an independent witness. A bare signature or the phrase 'against advice' proves nothing about what the patient actually understood.

quiz.q: A 26-year-old with a deformed, obviously painful femur insists nothing else hurts after a car crash. Why is a focused exam of the leg inadequate?
choices: A distracting injury makes him an unreliable reporter, so injuries elsewhere can be silent
Because femur fractures always come with pelvic fractures
Because focused exams are never used in trauma
Because he cannot consent to a focused exam
quiz.why: Severe pain in one place owns the patient's attention and masks pain elsewhere, which is one of the five unreliability criteria. Focused exams are valid in trauma, just not on an unreliable reporter with a significant mechanism.

quiz.q: A 34-year-old has a fever of 39.1 C and a headache. Which two exam items are most important to add?
choices: Pelvis stability and distal pulses
Skin fully exposed for a rash, and neck stiffness
Abdominal quadrants and last oral intake
Grip strength in both hands
quiz.why: Fever with headache raises meningitis, where a rash and neck stiffness are the findings that change urgency and isolation precautions. Pelvis, abdomen, and grip strength do not address the worst thing this combination can be.

quiz.q: A 45-year-old passed out at work and is now alert and oriented with no complaints. What does he still need?
choices: Only a blood pressure and a ride home
Only a cardiac history
Glucose, pulse rate and regularity, blood pressure, orientation, and a head-to-toe for injuries from the fall
A focused abdominal exam only
quiz.why: Syncope means the brain lost perfusion, so you look for a rhythm problem, bleeding, or low sugar, and you also look for what he hit on the way down. Feeling fine now does not undo a head strike that has not declared itself yet.

quiz.q: A 7-year-old has a heart rate of 150 after a bicycle crash. How should this be read?
choices: Normal for a 7-year-old at rest
Bradycardia for age
Irrelevant if the child is talking
Above the normal range of 70 to 120 for this age, and a possible early sign of shock or pain
quiz.why: The 6 to 12 year band runs 70 to 120, so 150 is tachycardia that needs an explanation such as pain, fear, fever, or blood loss. Children hold pressure while the rate climbs, so a normal blood pressure does not make the rate harmless.

quiz.q: An 81-year-old with pneumonia has a temperature of 36.2 C. What does the normal temperature tell you?
choices: Almost nothing, because older adults often fail to mount a fever with serious infection
That infection is ruled out
That she is likely hypothermic from the environment
That antibiotics have already been effective
quiz.why: Aging blunts thermoregulation, so serious infection frequently arrives with a normal or even low temperature. Using a normal reading to exclude infection in an elder is the same error as trusting a normal heart rate on a beta blocker.

quiz.q: A 77-year-old with hearing aids out cannot follow your questions in a noisy room. What is the best adjustment?
choices: Shout each question until she responds
Put her hearing aids and glasses in, face her directly, and speak slowly in a lower pitch
Direct all questions to the family instead
Document that the patient is confused
quiz.why: Age-related hearing loss hits high frequencies first, so shouting raises pitch and makes it worse. Restoring her devices and facing her preserves both the history and an accurate mental status, which shouting and bypassing her destroy.

quiz.q: An infant is quiet, makes no eye contact, and does not protest when you palpate her abdomen firmly. How should you read this?
choices: Reassuring, because she is calm and cooperative
Expected for a sleeping infant
Worrying, because a child too quiet to protest an exam is a sick child
Evidence that the abdomen is not tender
quiz.why: Vigorous protest is the reassuring finding in a small child; silence and absent gaze are abnormal appearance on the pediatric assessment triangle. Reading her lack of reaction as cooperation or as a negative abdominal exam misses a sick infant.

quiz.q: A patient has been down on a hard floor for an estimated 9 hours. Beyond the cause of the collapse, what else should you expect?
choices: Nothing else, down time only affects stroke eligibility
Only dehydration
Only a higher chance of aspiration
Pressure injury to dependent skin, muscle breakdown, and hypothermia
quiz.why: Hours of immobility on a hard surface damage skin and muscle and leach heat, all of which matter to the receiving team. Stroke windows and aspiration are real, but they are not the whole cost of a long down time.

quiz.q: A pill bottle for 60 oxycodone tablets was filled 4 days ago and contains 6 tablets. Why does this matter?
choices: The fill date and remaining count estimate how much was taken and over what period, which is history the patient cannot give you
It proves the patient has a substance use disorder
It determines the naloxone dose exactly
It has no clinical value and should be left at the scene
quiz.why: Counting pills against the fill date brackets the exposure, which shapes how long the hospital watches for re-sedation. It is not a character judgment, it does not set a dose, and leaving it behind destroys information nobody can recover later.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient has hot, dry skin, a temperature of 40.6 C, and was found in a closed apartment during a heat wave. What does the dry skin add?
choices: It rules out a heat emergency because sweating is required
It suggests heat stroke, where the sweating mechanism has failed, and this is a true emergency
It indicates hypoglycemia
It points to opioid toxicity
quiz.why: Loss of sweating with a very high core temperature and altered mental status is heat stroke, not a milder heat illness. Low sugar produces cool clammy skin and opioids produce pinpoint pupils with slow breathing, neither of which fits.

quiz.q: A multi-system trauma patient has an open chest wound that bubbles with each breath. What is the correct EMT action?
choices: Pack the wound tightly with gauze
Leave it open so air can escape
Apply a vented or three-sided occlusive dressing and monitor for worsening breathing
Apply a tourniquet above the wound
quiz.why: A vented or three-sided seal stops air entering during inspiration while letting trapped air escape, which reduces the risk of creating a tension pneumothorax. Packing a chest wound, leaving it open, and tourniquets to the torso are all wrong.

quiz.q: You reach a critical trauma patient at 1507 and leave the scene at 1524. What should your documentation include?
choices: Nothing, scene time is not documented
Only the departure time
Only the dispatch time
The specific reason the scene time exceeded 10 minutes, such as entrapment or extrication
quiz.why: Seventeen minutes is well past the benchmark, and the standard is that you can state exactly why. Times alone without a reason leave a reviewer to assume the delay was avoidable.

quiz.q: During critical trauma care, when should a mid-shaft femur fracture be splinted on scene rather than en route?
choices: When the limb is pulseless or the patient must be moved through an extrication
Always, before any movement
Never, splinting is a hospital task
Only after a complete set of vital signs
quiz.why: A pulseless limb and extrication are the two reasons that justify spending scene minutes on a splint. Routine on-scene splinting trades time against the 10-minute benchmark, and splinting itself is squarely in EMT scope.

quiz.q: Which trauma alert report gives the receiving team the most usable information in ten seconds?
choices: We have a bad one coming in, pretty messed up, be ready
Twenty-four-year-old restrained driver, high-speed head-on, tourniquet on the left thigh at 1418, HR 138, BP 92/76, GCS 13, ETA 6 minutes
Car accident, young guy, we will explain when we get there
Trauma patient, vitals soft, hurt his leg, ETA soon
quiz.why: Mechanism, injury, intervention with a time, numbers, and an arrival time let the team assemble before the doors open. Adjectives such as bad, soft, and messed up carry no decision-making content at all.

quiz.q: Serial vitals: BP 140/80 then 134/88 then 128/100, HR 78 then 96 then 118, skin now pale. Calculate the pulse pressure trend and interpret it.
choices: 60 to 46 to 28, improving
60 to 46 to 28, no clinical meaning
60 to 46 to 28, a narrowing pulse pressure with rising tachycardia, which is compensated shock
60 to 46 to 28, which indicates a cuff that is too large
quiz.why: Systolic minus diastolic narrows from 60 to 28 while the rate climbs 40 beats and the skin goes pale, which is vasoconstriction compensating for volume loss. A cuff error would not produce a smooth trend across three sets that matches the skin findings.

quiz.q: You give oral glucose to a hypoglycemic patient at 1430. When and what do you reassess?
choices: At 1445 only, on the 15-minute schedule
On hospital arrival, when a repeat glucose can be done
Only if the patient complains of new symptoms
Immediately and then every few minutes: mental status, ability to protect the airway, and a repeat glucose
quiz.why: Every intervention earns an immediate check of whether it worked, and with glucose that means mental status first, since a patient whose level of consciousness is falling can no longer swallow safely. Waiting for a schedule or for the hospital hides a failed treatment.

quiz.q: A head-injured patient's vitals move from HR 96 and BP 140/84 to HR 52 and BP 200/96 with irregular breathing. What does this mean for the head of the stretcher?
choices: Elevate the head about 30 degrees if there is no spinal contraindication and the pressure allows
Place the patient in steep head-down position to improve brain blood flow
Keep the patient flat and hyperventilate at 30 per minute
Position does not affect intracranial pressure
quiz.why: Cushing's triad signals rising intracranial pressure, and head elevation helps venous drainage from the skull. Head-down worsens pressure, and routine hyperventilation is harmful because it constricts vessels and reduces brain blood flow.

quiz.q: A 22-year-old with a chest injury speaks only Haitian Creole and no interpreter is immediately available. What is the best approach?
choices: Assume he cannot give a history and skip it
Use a phone interpreter service, closed yes-or-no questions with gestures, and weight the physical exam more heavily until an interpreter is on the line
Have a bystander who speaks some Creole translate everything including the risks of refusal
Speak English slowly and loudly
quiz.why: A language barrier makes the patient an unreliable historian by circumstance, so you get a real interpreter and lean on what you can observe in the meantime. Bystander translation is unreliable for consent and risk discussions, and volume does not create comprehension.

quiz.q: An agitated patient is pacing between you and the only door of a small bedroom. What is the immediate problem?
choices: Your report will be incomplete
You need a second blood pressure
Your exit is blocked, so you reposition toward the door or leave and stage for police
He will not be able to hear your questions
quiz.why: Keeping the exit behind you is the rule that makes de-escalation survivable, and a blocked door is a safety failure, not a communication one. Assessment and documentation are irrelevant if you cannot leave the room.

quiz.q: A 5-year-old asks if the blood pressure cuff will hurt. What is the best answer?
choices: It will not hurt at all, I promise
Do not worry about it
You will not even feel it
It is going to squeeze your arm tight for a few seconds, like a big hug, then it lets go
quiz.why: An honest, concrete description keeps the child's trust when the sensation arrives. A promise that something will not hurt costs you every future answer and burns the next provider too.

quiz.q: Which handoff element most directly builds the receiving team's next five minutes?
choices: One sentence naming what you are worried about
The patient's insurance information
A complete list of every body region you palpated
The names of the crew members
quiz.why: The concern sentence tells the team what room, what team, and what equipment to assemble. Insurance and crew names are administrative, and an exhaustive exam recital buries the pertinent findings in noise.

quiz.q: You write 'patient improved after oxygen' with no times attached. What is the deficiency?
choices: It is too brief for a narrative
Without timestamps on the before and after findings, the improvement cannot be proven or compared
Oxygen does not need to be documented
Improvement should never be charted
quiz.why: Trend is the entire information content of serial assessment, and a trend without a clock is an assertion. The fix is timed values on both sides: speaking three words at 1408, full sentences at 1416.

quiz.q: Which of the following is the MIST format used for?
choices: Recording a refusal
Documenting a scene size-up
Giving a trauma handoff: mechanism, injuries found, signs including vitals, treatment given
Taking a pain history
quiz.why: MIST is the trauma container for the handoff, matching what a trauma team needs in order. Refusals, size-ups, and pain histories have their own structures, and OPQRST is the one for pain.

quiz.q: You are the emergency department tech receiving a crew's report on a found-down patient. Which two facts should you write down first?
choices: The patient's address and date of birth
The crew's unit number and the dispatch time
The current heart rate and oxygen saturation
The estimated down time and the first set of vitals
quiz.why: Down time and the first vitals exist only in the crew's heads and vanish the moment they leave, while current vitals are already on your monitor. Demographics and unit numbers can be retrieved from the chart at any point.

quiz.q: A candidate performs a flawless but silent assessment, treats everything correctly, and finishes early. What is the likely score?
choices: Low, because unspoken assessments and findings cannot be awarded points
High, because speed demonstrates competence
High, because the evaluator can infer the findings
Unaffected, since narration is optional
quiz.why: The sheet scores observed and verbalized actions, so silent work reads as omission no matter how good it is. This is why clinically strong candidates are among the most common failures at this station.

quiz.q: At the station, a patient is breathing 6 times per minute. The candidate applies a nasal cannula at 4 L/min and continues. What is the outcome?
choices: Full credit, because oxygen was provided
Critical failure for not providing appropriate ventilation when indicated
One point deducted for device selection
No effect, because the device choice is the candidate's judgment
quiz.why: A rate of 6 is respiratory failure and needs bag-valve-mask ventilation at 1 breath every 6 seconds, not supplemental oxygen through a cannula. Failure to provide appropriate ventilation when indicated is a listed critical criterion, not a deduction.

quiz.q: Which statement earns the most points on the skill sheet?
choices: Checking the pulse silently and moving on
Saying 'I am checking circulation' with no finding stated
Saying 'Radial pulse present, rapid and weak, skin cool and pale; this patient is in compensated shock and is a high transport priority'
Saying 'The patient looks bad' after the exam
quiz.why: Stating the action, the finding, and the meaning together earns the assessment point and demonstrates the priority decision. Naming an action without its result, or an impression without findings, leaves the evaluator nothing to score.

quiz.q: Which of these is a quiet point-loser rather than a critical failure at the assessment station?
choices: Moving a patient with a suspected spinal injury without stabilization
Never taking or verbalizing BSI precautions
Finding heavy bleeding and continuing without treating it
Taking one blood pressure and never obtaining a second set
quiz.why: Missing the reassessment costs the points tied to it but does not by itself end the station. Unstabilized spinal movement, absent BSI, and an untreated life threat are all listed critical failures that end it regardless of other points.
